cards.meaning: Spending or using resources in a wasteful, excessively extravagant way.
cards.nuance: It is stronger and more disapproving than “expensive” or “extravagant.” It is often used about irresponsible spending, consumption or use of resources.

uses.sentence: The agency’s profligate travel budget helped explain why the project ran out of money.
uses.tip: Use it when criticising spending that seems careless or excessive.

uses.sentence: Our weekend spending felt profligate after we realised we had booked three expensive dinners.
uses.tip: It adds a strong, slightly judgemental note to a complaint about excess.

uses.sentence: The report criticises the company’s profligate spending on consultants and international events.
uses.tip: This is a formal and forceful choice for serious criticism of waste.

origin.summary: From Latin profligatus, meaning “ruined” or “wasted,” originally associated with being driven down or destroyed.

timeline.text: Profligatus develops from profligare, meaning “to drive down, ruin or waste.”
English adopts the word with senses involving ruin, waste and excessive spending.
Its main meaning is recklessly extravagant or wasteful, especially with money.

cards.pitfall: It is more critical than “lavish,” which can describe generosity or luxury without disapproval. “Profligate” can also sound moralistic, so choose it carefully.

cards.meaning: A natural tendency to behave in a particular way or prefer doing something.
cards.nuance: Often suggests a pattern that is noticeable but not always deliberate. It can sound slightly more formal than “tendency” and may imply a negative tendency when used about unwanted behaviour.

uses.sentence: The product team has a propensity to prioritise speed over accessibility, so we should test the new flow with disabled users.
uses.tip: Use it when describing a recurring tendency within a person or team.

uses.sentence: I have a propensity to order the same dish whenever I see it on the menu.
uses.tip: It works naturally when describing a personal habit, especially one you are slightly self-aware about.

uses.sentence: The findings show a clear propensity among younger respondents to share news through messaging apps.
uses.tip: A useful formal word for patterns identified in data or research.

origin.summary: From Latin propensio, meaning a leaning or inclination, and related to propensus, “inclined towards”.

timeline.text: The root propensus meant inclined or leaning towards, and propensio meant an inclination.
The word enters English with meanings connected to inclination and natural tendency.
It is used for noticeable tendencies in behaviour, preferences or patterns found in data.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse it with “propaganda”; “propensity” is a tendency, while “propaganda” is material intended to influence opinion.

cards.meaning: Ready and eager to fight, argue or take an aggressive approach.
cards.nuance: It suggests an active desire for confrontation, not merely a forceful personality. It can describe a person, an attitude or a demanding, combative negotiating style.

uses.sentence: The department became pugnacious when managers rejected every request for additional staff.
uses.tip: Use it for a noticeably hostile or confrontational response.

uses.sentence: My uncle gets pugnacious whenever anyone questions his advice.
uses.tip: It sounds more critical than simply argumentative, because it implies eagerness for conflict.

uses.sentence: Both sides adopted a pugnacious tone, exchanging sharp accusations instead of addressing the proposal.
uses.tip: The word fits formal reporting when you want to emphasize an openly hostile tone.

origin.summary: From Latin pugnaciousus, meaning ‘fond of fighting’, from pugnare, ‘to fight’, and pugnax, ‘eager for battle’.

timeline.text: Pugnaciousus is formed from pugnax, ‘eager for battle’, and a suffix meaning ‘characterized by’.
The word enters English in a literal sense, meaning inclined or skilled in fighting.
Its use broadens to describe argumentative, aggressive behaviour and a hostile tone.

cards.pitfall: Use it for people or attitudes that actively seek conflict; it is stronger and more formal than simply ‘aggressive’.

cards.meaning: Greedy for money, power or possessions, often taking more than you need or deserve.
cards.nuance: Strongly negative and usually more literary than everyday words such as “greedy.” It can describe a person, an organisation or a demanding appetite.

uses.sentence: The vendor’s rapacious pricing left us with no room to negotiate.
uses.tip: Stronger than “expensive”; it suggests unreasonable greed.

uses.sentence: My cousin was rapacious with the buffet and returned home with three extra plates.
uses.tip: Adds a humorous, slightly exaggerated sense of greed.

uses.sentence: The takeover was driven by rapacious ambition rather than a sound long-term strategy.
uses.tip: A forceful choice for formal criticism of excessive corporate appetite.

origin.summary: From Latin rapax, meaning “seizing” or “greedy,” based on rapere, “to seize or grab.” The word entered English in the 1600s.

timeline.text: Rapax develops from rapere, “to seize or grab,” and comes to mean “greedy” or “predatory.”
Rapacious enters English in the sense of greedy or excessively demanding.
It chiefly describes greed for money, power, possessions or food.

cards.pitfall: It can sound very forceful, so choose a gentler word such as “greedy” when you do not want strong criticism.

cards.meaning: Stubbornly resistant to authority, rules, instructions or attempts to cooperate.
cards.nuance: Stronger and more formal than “stubborn,” suggesting a person or thing repeatedly refuses to yield. It is often used for difficult students, employees, animals or machinery.

uses.sentence: The recalcitrant department head refused to approve the new workflow despite two meetings.
uses.tip: Use it when resistance is persistent, not merely a normal disagreement.

uses.sentence: Our recalcitrant nephew had decided that no reasonable request would earn a yes.
uses.tip: A slightly humorous but firm way to describe someone being extremely uncooperative.

uses.sentence: The recalcitrant engine remained out of service until an engineer replaced its damaged control module.
uses.tip: It can describe machinery that will not work or respond as expected.

origin.summary: From Latin recalcitrare, meaning “to be stubborn or refuse to yield,” originally associated with a horse’s heels and the lime used to make a path slippery.

timeline.text: Recalcitrare developed from calx, meaning “lime,” and a root associated with slipping or resisting pressure.
The word entered English with the meaning “stubbornly resistant to control or authority.”
It describes people, animals and machines that persistently refuse to cooperate.

cards.pitfall: It is stronger than “reluctant,” which may describe simple hesitation. Recalcitrant suggests firm, repeated resistance to pressure or authority.

cards.register: Common at work and in serious conversation
cards.meaning: Acting without enough thought about the risks or possible harm your actions could cause.
cards.nuance: It is a strong criticism and can suggest that someone ignored obvious dangers. It is often used when poor judgement leads to damage, danger or unnecessary risk.

uses.where: Safety review · discussing a rushed decision
uses.sentence: Skipping the final checks was reckless, especially when the equipment can damage the whole production line.
uses.tip: Use it for a decision that showed a serious lack of care or judgement.

uses.sentence: It was reckless to send that message while you were angry, so give yourself some time before replying.
uses.tip: It fits actions that may hurt someone or make a difficult situation worse.

uses.sentence: Management called the changes reckless because they exposed employees and customers to avoidable harm.
uses.tip: Pair it with a clear consequence or detail to make the criticism specific.

origin.summary: From Old English words meaning “without care”: a word for care combined with a prefix meaning “without.” The modern form appeared in the 1500s.

timeline.text: Related to Old English words meaning “care” and “without care.”
The modern form emerges, describing behaviour marked by a lack of care.
It means acting without proper regard for danger, risk or consequences.

cards.pitfall: Careless is often milder and more general; reckless suggests a clearer disregard for serious risk or consequences.

cards.meaning: Able to be trusted to do what is expected, work consistently, or perform properly.
cards.nuance: It often suggests steadiness and dependability rather than exceptional skill. It can describe people, systems, methods, vehicles, news sources and more.

uses.sentence: Priya is reliable, so I’m giving her the client report before Friday.
uses.tip: Use it to praise someone’s dependability in a specific, practical way.

uses.sentence: The earlier train is more reliable when you’re going to meet friends for dinner.
uses.tip: Useful when discussing transport, services or anything that needs to work consistently.

uses.sentence: This printer is less reliable than the cheaper model, but it produces better photos.
uses.tip: A clear choice when a product needs to perform consistently over time.

origin.summary: From Latin reliabilis, meaning trustworthy or dependable, based on fidus, meaning faithful or trustworthy.

timeline.text: Reliabilis is formed from fidere, ‘to trust’, and means trustworthy.
The word enters English in the sense of trustworthy or dependable.
It describes anything that can be trusted to work consistently or do what is expected.

cards.pitfall: Reliable means dependable, not necessarily the best or most powerful option.

cards.meaning: Failing to show enough care, effort, or responsibility in carrying out a duty.
cards.nuance: It suggests negligence rather than an accidental mistake. The word is most natural in serious or official contexts.

uses.sentence: The auditor said the team had been remiss in recording the safety checks.
uses.tip: Use it for a clear failure to meet a responsibility.

uses.sentence: We were remiss in welcoming the new neighbours, so let’s organise a proper introduction.
uses.tip: It can acknowledge a social duty that people did not fulfil.

uses.sentence: The landlord was remiss in maintaining the heating system and failed to respond to repeated complaints.
uses.tip: This gives formal reports a direct way to describe neglected duties.

origin.summary: From Latin remissus, meaning ‘sent back’ or ‘slackened’, and later ‘careless or negligent’. It entered English in the 1500s.

timeline.text: Remissus develops from remittere, meaning ‘send back’ or ‘release’, and comes to mean slack or careless.
The word enters English with senses connected to release, pardon and carelessness.
It is mainly used formally for neglecting a duty or responsibility.

cards.pitfall: Use it for neglected duties, not simply a lack of skill or an unavoidable mistake.

cards.meaning: A collection of skills, ideas or performances that someone can draw on.
cards.nuance: Often suggests a wide range of well-practised abilities. It can also refer to the material a performer regularly performs.

uses.where: Team workshop · planning for a new client
uses.sentence: Our support team’s repertoire of solutions is broad enough to handle almost any onboarding problem.
uses.tip: Use it when discussing the range of skills or approaches someone has developed.

uses.sentence: Her jazz repertoire includes both timeless standards and recent reinterpretations.
uses.tip: It is especially natural when talking about songs or material a performer knows.

uses.sentence: He brought an impressive repertoire of experience to his first leadership role.
uses.tip: Use it for a professional range of knowledge, techniques or proven methods.

origin.summary: Borrowed from French répertoire, originally meaning a catalogue or index, and ultimately related to Latin reperire, ‘to find out’.

timeline.text: Reperire develops the sense of finding or discovering something available.
French répertoire means a catalogue or inventory of items.
The word reaches English and begins referring to a collection of artistic material.
It means a range of skills, works or performances someone can use.

cards.pitfall: In British English, repertoire is common; repertoire is also accepted but is less usual.

cards.meaning: Not freely showing emotions, opinions or personal information.
cards.nuance: It can describe someone who is quiet and self-controlled, or simply formal with strangers. The word may sound mildly critical, especially when you imply that someone is holding something back.

uses.sentence: She was initially reserved, but opened up once she got to know the team.
uses.tip: This sounds neutral and can describe someone who takes time to settle in.

uses.sentence: He stayed reserved during the first course, then joined in when the conversation turned to football.
uses.tip: Use it for quiet behaviour rather than unfriendliness.

uses.sentence: Your reserved style helps in negotiations, though colleagues may find it difficult to read your mood.
uses.tip: Pair it with style, manner or personality; avoid using it as a vague criticism.

origin.summary: From Old French reserve, meaning kept back or saved, from the Latin reservare. English later developed the senses of keeping something for later and behaving with restraint.

timeline.text: Reserve means kept back, saved or set aside.
The word develops senses including set aside for another purpose and kept in restraint.
Reserved most often describes a quiet, self-controlled person or manner.

cards.pitfall: Reserved can also mean set aside or booked, as in a reserved seat. The past tense of reserve is also spelled reserved.

cards.meaning: Showing firm determination to make a decision and continue until it is achieved.
cards.nuance: It suggests steadiness and a refusal to be shaken by difficulty. It is especially useful when describing leaders, decisions, or efforts that require firm commitment.

uses.where: Project meeting · deciding on a delay
uses.sentence: The team took a resolute approach to the deadline and agreed on three priorities for this week.
uses.tip: Use it to emphasize firm action without sounding aggressive.

uses.sentence: She was resolute about moving to another city, even though her friends were unsure.
uses.tip: It fits when describing someone’s firm, settled determination.

uses.sentence: The manager remained resolute when the project faced several unexpected setbacks.
uses.tip: It gives a formal note of praise for steady, determined leadership.

origin.summary: From Latin resolutus, meaning ‘unbound’ or ‘resolved’, based on solvere, ‘to loosen’ or ‘solve’.

timeline.text: Resolutus develops from resolvere, meaning ‘to untie’ or ‘solve’.
The word enters English, initially meaning free from ties or obstacles.
It takes on its modern sense of being firmly determined.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse it with resolute in the sense of being dissolved or broken; in modern English, it almost always means firmly determined.

cards.meaning: Able to solve problems creatively and make good use of the people, materials or opportunities available.
cards.nuance: It is a positive word that highlights ingenuity and adaptability, especially when conditions are difficult or unpredictable.

uses.where: Team meeting · solving a staffing shortage
uses.sentence: Mina was resourceful, training two new colleagues while keeping the project on schedule.
uses.tip: Use it to praise someone’s problem-solving skills and practical initiative.

uses.sentence: Our resourceful host turned a wrong turn into an afternoon exploring a nearby market.
uses.tip: It often describes people who stay calm and improvise when plans go wrong.

uses.sentence: She is a resourceful team member who can turn limited budgets into strong results.
uses.tip: It works well in evaluations when you want to emphasise adaptability rather than technical expertise.

origin.summary: Built from resource, meaning a source of help or support, plus the suffix -ful.

timeline.text: Resource comes through Old French from Latin resources, meaning sources or means of support.
Resourceful begins appearing in English with the sense of able to find ways to succeed.
It is mainly used to praise creativity, initiative and practical problem-solving.

cards.pitfall: Do not confuse resourceful with resourceful-looking; the word normally suggests a demonstrated ability to solve problems.

cards.meaning: Unwilling to talk freely about something, often because you are cautious or have been asked to keep it confidential.
cards.nuance: A negative word that suggests silence or guarded behaviour rather than simple shyness. It is especially useful when describing how someone handles sensitive information.

uses.sentence: The director was reticent about the merger, so we waited for an official announcement.
uses.tip: Use it for someone who deliberately avoids revealing information.

uses.where: Dinner party · asking about a new relationship
uses.sentence: He seemed reticent at first, but opened up once we moved away from the group.
uses.tip: It can describe reserved behaviour in a social setting without sounding openly rude.

uses.sentence: Although knowledgeable, she was reticent in meetings and rarely volunteered her opinions.
uses.tip: It is effective in formal reports when you need to comment on someone’s guarded communication style.

origin.summary: From Latin reticere, meaning ‘to keep silent’, formed from re-, ‘back’, and tacere, ‘to be silent’.

timeline.text: Reticere means ‘to keep silent’ or ‘to withhold speech’.
The word enters English in the sense of being reserved or reluctant to speak.
It describes someone who is cautious about speaking or revealing information.

cards.pitfall: Do not use it simply to mean shy; it usually implies deliberate caution or reluctance to speak.

cards.meaning: Making an exaggerated show of moral purity, goodness or religious devotion.
cards.nuance: It usually suggests that the person is self-righteous or more concerned with appearing virtuous than acting virtuously. It can describe either conscious hypocrisy or an outward performance that may hide ordinary behaviour.

uses.sentence: His sanctimonious response to the proposal made everyone uncomfortable.
uses.tip: Use it for a conspicuously self-righteous manner, not simply for having firm moral standards.

uses.sentence: She became sanctimonious and called everyone selfish for enjoying the party.
uses.tip: It is strong and usually carries criticism from the speaker.

uses.sentence: The article dismissed his sanctimonious campaign as moral theatre rather than genuine reform.
uses.tip: It works well in sharp commentary but may sound too forceful in a neutral report.

origin.summary: It comes through French from Latin sanctimonia, meaning holiness or reverence, originally associated with being holy or sacred.

timeline.text: Sanctimonia develops from words meaning holy, holiness or reverence.
The word enters English with the sense of showing reverence or moral seriousness.
It chiefly describes an exaggerated, often self-righteous display of virtue.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it for someone who is quietly devout or ethically strict; it usually implies a showy or judgemental attitude.

cards.meaning: To move quickly with short, hurried steps, often because of fear, excitement or urgency.
cards.nuance: It suggests light, nervous or bustling movement. As a noun, a scurry is a sudden burst of hurried activity.

uses.sentence: The interns scurry back to their desks when the director unexpectedly walks in.
uses.tip: Use it to suggest nervous, hurried movement rather than calm activity.

uses.sentence: Children scurry around the lawn while trying to find the hidden eggs.
uses.tip: It sounds natural for quick, playful movement, especially involving small animals or children.

uses.sentence: A scurry of activity fills the station as passengers search for the correct platform.
uses.tip: Use the noun for a sudden flurry of busy or slightly chaotic activity.

origin.summary: The exact source is uncertain. The word may come from an obsolete English verb, possibly influenced by Old French escorrer, meaning ‘to hasten’.

timeline.text: Scurry appears in English with the sense of moving in short, hurried steps.
A noun meaning a sudden rush or bustle develops alongside the verb.
The word becomes common in descriptions of nervous people, small animals and busy places.

cards.pitfall: Scurry usually emphasizes quick, light movement or a flurry of activity; hurry focuses more directly on speed or urgency.

cards.meaning: Showing too much eagerness to obey or please someone, often in a humble or degrading way.
cards.nuance: The tone is critical: it suggests obedience that has lost self-respect. It is stronger and more negative than simply being respectful.

uses.sentence: He was servile toward senior managers but confident when speaking to junior colleagues.
uses.tip: Use it when respect appears excessive, unequal or driven by fear.

uses.where: Dinner party · reacting to a guest
uses.sentence: His servile agreement with every opinion made the conversation feel uncomfortable.
uses.tip: It can describe behaviour that seems ingratiating rather than genuinely enthusiastic.

uses.where: Review · describing a manager's leadership style
uses.sentence: Her style was supportive, but some employees disliked how servile it could become.
uses.tip: Use it carefully in formal criticism, especially with evidence of unequal treatment.

origin.summary: From Latin servilis, meaning ‘of or relating to a slave’, which developed into the idea of submissive obedience.

timeline.text: Servilis is derived from servus, meaning ‘slave’, and refers to being enslaved or subordinate.
The word enters English with meanings connected with slavery, bondage and subjection.
It mainly describes excessively submissive behaviour toward someone with power or authority.

cards.pitfall: Servile is more critical than deferential: deferential can be a respectful courtesy, while servile suggests excessive obedience.

cards.meaning: Suggesting evil, danger, or a threatening hidden intention.
cards.nuance: It often creates a dark, suspenseful atmosphere. The word can describe a person’s appearance or apparent motives, so it may sound dramatic or melodramatic.

uses.sentence: His sudden interest in our customer data felt sinister, and nobody trusted his explanation.
uses.tip: Use it when something suggests deliberate harm rather than an ordinary mistake.

uses.sentence: The abandoned house had a sinister atmosphere, especially when the lights began to flicker.
uses.tip: It is effective for stories, warnings and descriptions that create unease.

uses.sentence: The investigator sensed that the stranger’s interest in the old diary was sinister.
uses.tip: Pair it with atmosphere, motive, presence or rumour to build tension.

origin.summary: From Latin sinister, meaning “left.” Left-hand signs became associated with bad luck in Roman thinking, which helped give the word its sense of something evil or threatening.

timeline.text: Sinister means “left,” and signs on the left came to be regarded as unlucky.
The word enters English with meanings connected with evil, misfortune and unfavourable omens.
It mainly describes danger, menace or an appearance of hidden evil intent.

cards.pitfall: It often carries a deliberately dark or dramatic tone, so choose a plain adjective for minor concerns.

cards.meaning: Untidy or careless, especially in appearance, organisation or handling of tasks.
cards.nuance: It sounds negative and can seem quite harsh. In professional writing, “untidy” or “disorganised” may be more tactful.

uses.sentence: The slovenly arrangement of files made it difficult to find the latest version.
uses.tip: Use it for visible disorder that suggests poor care or organisation.

uses.sentence: Sorry the place looks slovenly; I haven't had time to tidy up.
uses.tip: It can describe a room, appearance or person, but it may embarrass the person you are describing.

uses.sentence: His slovenly record-keeping led to several important documents being misplaced.
uses.tip: Keep the tone factual; “disorganised” may sound less personal in formal writing.

origin.summary: From the now-obsolete English word “sloven”, meaning careless or negligent, probably related to “slow”. It later became a familiar criticism of untidy people or places.

timeline.text: “Slovenly” develops from an older form meaning careless or negligent.
The word becomes established in everyday English, especially for untidy appearance and behaviour.
It remains a direct, slightly harsh way to describe untidiness or carelessness.

cards.pitfall: “Slovenly” can describe either untidiness or careless work; it is not limited to someone’s appearance.

cards.meaning: Dirty, unpleasant, or morally disreputable.
cards.nuance: It can describe physical dirtiness, but it is also used for dishonest or shameful behaviour. The word sounds stronger and more judgemental than “dirty” or “shameful.”

uses.sentence: The company ignored the sordid details of how the contract had been won.
uses.tip: Use it for conduct that is both morally wrong and unpleasant to consider.

uses.sentence: She refused to discuss the sordid argument they had had in public.
uses.tip: It adds a strong sense of moral disapproval to a situation.

uses.sentence: The report revealed a sordid network of private deals and concealed payments.
uses.tip: It is especially effective in formal writing about corruption or disgraceful conduct.

origin.summary: From Latin sordidus, meaning ‘dirty’ or ‘disreputable’, related to sordes, ‘dirt’, and sordere, ‘to be dirty’. The word originally described physical filth before developing its moral sense.

timeline.text: Sordidus meant ‘dirty’, ‘filthy’, or ‘disreputable’.
The word entered English with meanings connected with dirt, filth, and disgrace.
It is mainly used for morally shameful or deeply disreputable things.

cards.pitfall: It is stronger and more judgemental than “dirty”; use it for something especially shameful, not for ordinary messiness.

cards.meaning: Done naturally and without planning beforehand, often because the moment calls for it.
cards.nuance: It suggests an honest, immediate reaction rather than a carefully arranged performance. It can also mean someone who readily acts, joins in or offers ideas without hesitation.

uses.sentence: Her spontaneous offer to help unblocked the meeting when our supplier raised an urgent issue.
uses.tip: Often describes quick, willing action that helps a situation.

uses.sentence: After mentioning the concert, we made a spontaneous decision to buy tickets and go that night.
uses.tip: Natural for a decision made on impulse rather than after careful planning.

uses.sentence: Thank you for your spontaneous support; it made the event feel warm and welcoming.
uses.tip: Praises something done quickly and generously without advance notice.

origin.summary: From Latin spontaneus, meaning ‘of one’s own accord’, which developed from sponte, ‘of one’s own will’.

timeline.text: Spontaneus develops from sponte, ‘of one’s own accord’, describing voluntary or self-directed action.
The word enters English in senses connected with voluntary action and things done of one’s own accord.
Takes on its modern sense of being done without prior planning.
Commonly describes spontaneous decisions, reactions, gestures and offers of help.

cards.pitfall: Don’t assume spontaneous always means impulsive or careless; it can also describe prompt, generous action that works well.

cards.register: Common at work and in formal discussion
cards.meaning: Showing firm loyalty, belief or support for a person, cause or position.
cards.nuance: It suggests steady commitment, not merely a temporary preference. It can also describe someone who firmly rejects something, such as a violent or harmful idea.

uses.sentence: She was a staunch supporter of the new security policy from the start.
uses.tip: Use it for strong, steady support, especially of a person, cause or decision.

uses.sentence: He remains a staunch defender of environmental protections despite the criticism.
uses.tip: This sounds committed and principled; use a milder word for casual agreement.

uses.sentence: The company has been a staunch defender of customer privacy for more than a decade.
uses.tip: It works well before nouns such as defender, ally, supporter and advocate.

origin.summary: From Old French estanch, meaning firm or secure, originally connected with stopping or closing something. Its modern sense of firmly committed developed in English.

timeline.text: The word appears in senses connected with being firm, fixed or secure.
It develops the meaning of being firmly loyal or committed.
It describes strong, steady support or firm opposition.

cards.pitfall: Use stanch for the less common variant spelling, but keep staunch when describing firm loyalty or opposition.

cards.meaning: Firmly committed to a purpose, principle, or person and unwilling to waver despite difficulty.
cards.nuance: It describes lasting loyalty or resolve, often with an approving tone. It is stronger and more personal than steady.

uses.sentence: Maya remained steadfast in defending the plan even when the launch was postponed.
uses.tip: Use it to describe firm commitment when circumstances become difficult.

uses.where: Dinner with friends · supporting a friend
uses.sentence: He was steadfast in his support, showing up whenever she needed him.
uses.tip: It fits naturally when describing dependable support or loyalty.

uses.where: Letter to a mentor · expressing thanks
uses.sentence: Thank you for being steadfast in your encouragement throughout my first year.
uses.tip: Use it in appreciative writing to recognise consistent support or commitment.

origin.summary: From Old English stedefæst, a compound of stede, meaning a place or position, and fæst, meaning firm, fast, or secure.

timeline.text: Stedefæst appears with the sense of firm, stable, or securely fixed.
The word develops into forms such as stedfast and eventually steadfast.
It mainly describes firm loyalty, resolve, or commitment.

cards.pitfall: Don’t confuse steadfast with steady: steadfast stresses firm commitment, while steady often stresses calmness or consistency.

cards.meaning: Requiring exact obedience to rules, standards or instructions.
cards.nuance: It describes people who set firm limits and situations where precise conditions are required. It can sound careful and dependable, but sometimes overly severe.

uses.sentence: Our release process is strict, so every change needs approval before deployment.
uses.tip: Use it for firm, clearly defined rules rather than simply difficult tasks.

uses.sentence: My parents are strict about arriving on time, even for a casual dinner.
uses.tip: It can describe a demanding upbringing or a rule that allows little flexibility.

uses.where: Email to a client · clarifying requirements
uses.sentence: Please review the strict criteria for this role and include every requested example.
uses.tip: Often used before requirements, standards, rules or deadlines to emphasize precision.

origin.summary: From Latin strictus, meaning drawn tight or closely bound, through Old French estroit. The word originally referred to something held tightly or closely.

timeline.text: Strictus meant drawn tight, close or exact.
Estroit carried the sense of being tight, narrow or closely constrained.
The word entered English and developed its modern sense of demanding exact obedience.

cards.pitfall: Strict is broader and more everyday. Stringent is more formal and often describes detailed rules, controls or requirements.

cards.meaning: Behaving as though you are more important or clever than other people.
cards.nuance: It describes a haughty, self-important manner and often implies contempt for others. It is strongly negative and sounds more formal than everyday words such as “arrogant.”

uses.sentence: His supercilious tone made it difficult for the rest of us to suggest alternatives.
uses.tip: Use it for behaviour that seems arrogant and dismissive, especially toward colleagues.

uses.sentence: She became supercilious whenever someone else received praise for their work.
uses.tip: It fits when someone displays pride or disdain that makes others uncomfortable.

uses.sentence: His ideas were useful, but his supercilious manner damaged the team's trust in him.
uses.tip: Pair it with manner, tone or attitude when criticising a person’s behaviour.

origin.summary: From Latin superciliosus, meaning “haughty” or “raising the eyebrow,” originally associated with pride expressed through the eyebrows.

timeline.text: Superciliosus develops from supercilium, meaning “eyebrow” and, by extension, a haughty expression.
The word enters English with the sense of haughty or disdainful.
It remains a formal word for behaviour that is arrogant and self-important.

cards.pitfall: Do not confuse it with “imperious,” which can mean domineering or commanding, not necessarily contemptuous of others.

cards.meaning: Someone who praises a powerful person to gain favour or avoid displeasing them.
cards.nuance: The word is strongly critical and suggests insincere flattery rather than genuine admiration. It is often used in politics, workplaces and arguments about influence.

uses.sentence: He agreed with every decision because he was a sycophant, not because he thought the plan worked.
uses.tip: Use it for habitual, self-serving praise, not ordinary politeness.

uses.sentence: Her compliments sounded sincere, but some people called her a sycophant once they saw how quickly she changed her opinions.
uses.tip: It carries judgement, so explain the behaviour if you are not sure it fits.

uses.sentence: The culture rewarded sycophants who repeated the leader’s ideas without adding any useful criticism.
uses.tip: Plural works well when describing a pattern within a group.

origin.summary: The familiar story that a sycophant informed on people who stole figs is a myth. The real origin is an Ancient Greek word for an informer or slanderer, later applied to deceitful flatterers.

timeline.text: Sykophantes referred to an informer or slanderer, originally someone who made accusations for selfish or dishonest reasons.
The word entered English through French and Latin, retaining the sense of a malicious informer.
Its meaning broadened to include people who flatter others for personal advantage.
It remains a hostile term for an insincere flatterer, especially around power and status.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it for someone giving a thoughtful compliment; the word implies exaggeration and a hidden motive.
